conclusions.statement: The article concludes that U.S. military escalation was measurably producing the opposite of reopening Hormuz.

analysis_decomposition.decomposition_note: The traffic-collapse numbers can be substantially correct while the claimed causal explanation remains unresolved or misleading. WOL therefore preserves the supported substrate and routes the causal bridge separately for Claims Forensics review.

factual_substrate.evidence_note: Independent S&P Global and Reuters reporting supports the broad traffic-collapse substrate while also warning that AIS-dark traffic makes raw visible counts incomplete.
factual_substrate.statement: Hormuz traffic fell drastically from roughly 125-130 daily prewar transits; independent reporting also recorded 11 ships on July 12 and very low subsequent traffic.

competing_explanations: Renewed Iranian attacks on commercial vessels directly increased perceived transit risk.
The U.S. blockade and wider U.S.-Iran escalation jointly depressed commercial confidence.
Insurer, charterer and crew risk decisions reduced traffic independently of any single strike wave.
AIS-dark traffic means visible transits undercount some actual movement.
inferential_bridges.evidentiary_issue: The sequence alone does not isolate U.S. strikes as the cause. Contemporary reporting also identifies renewed Iranian attacks on commercial vessels, blockade effects, insurer/crew risk, and AIS-dark transits as material contributors.
inferential_bridges.statement: Temporal correlation between renewed U.S. strike waves and lower visible ship counts is treated as evidence that the U.S. strikes themselves were producing the shutdown.
